question: Not the same clinical question, although both tasks are nominally three-class normal/MCI/dementia. P-269's classes are bands of the SLUMS screening score (Normal 25-30, MCI 20-24, dementia 0-19). The sample is 343 Saudi adults aged 60+ interviewed at COVID-19 vaccine centres, and no clinical diagnosis is made. P-95's classes are clinical diagnoses: AD by NINCDS-ADRDA, MCI by Petersen/NIA-AA, and matched healthy controls with no subjective complaint, 30 each, from a Novi Sad neurology clinic. The population behind the labels therefore differs: community attendees banded by a screening score against clinic patients with diagnosed AD and MCI. The channel is broadly shared on P-95's neuropsychological subset, since P-269 uses questionnaire items (demographics, sleep habits, medical history) and P-95 uses neuropsychological tests plus MRI. The population and label construct are not shared.
metric: Three-class accuracy in both. The class definitions differ (score bands against clinical diagnoses).

figures.P-269: SVM accuracy 93.3% for all patients (94.4% males, 95.5% females; the record cites the female subgroup). No interval is printed. The Table 3 confusion matrix for 'All' SVM sums to the whole sample: 173+11+1+5+110+0+1+5+37 = 343, and (173+110+37)/343 = 320/343 = 0.933. The 93.3% is therefore computed over all 343 participants, about 80% of whom were training cases (80/20 split), and is not a held-out estimate. As printed, the Wilson 95% interval on n = 343 is [0.901, 0.955]. If the figure were a held-out estimate on the 20% test split (n about 69), it would be [0.848, 0.972]: z^2/n = 0.0557; centre = (0.933 + 0.0278)/1.0557 = 0.910; half-width = 1.96*sqrt(0.933*0.067/69 + 3.8416/(4*69^2))/1.0557 = 0.0618.
figures.P-95: Three-class accuracy on all attributes ranges from 66.22% (LR) to 81.00% (naive Bayes) across seven default Weka classifiers. The best neuropsychological combination with SVM is 79.78%. These come from 10x10 stratified CV on 90 subjects (30/30/30). Wilson 95% for 0.81, n = 90: z^2/n = 0.0427; centre = (0.81 + 0.0213)/1.0427 = 0.797; half-width = 1.96*sqrt(0.81*0.19/90 + 3.8416/(4*8100))/1.0427 = 0.0804; interval [0.717, 0.878]. For 0.7978 the interval is [0.703, 0.868].

matched_figure_check: No matched figure exists. Neither paper reports a result under the other's label definition: P-269 has no clinically diagnosed classes and P-95 has no SLUMS bands. P-269 also has no cognitive-test or imaging predictors, and P-95 has no survey-only model. On the printed figures, 93.3% and 81.0% would exclude each other's intervals whichever n is used for P-269. That arithmetic does not matter while the classes are different constructs, and P-269's figure is not a validation estimate.
performance_validity: The Section 3.5 exclusion is not met on its letter: 93.3% (95.5% for the female subgroup) is below 0.97. P-269's female logistic model prints 100%, but that is not the compared figure. A separate validity problem applies: P-269's confusion matrices total the full sample (343 all, 233 male, 110 female), so its accuracies are computed largely on training data and are not internal-validation estimates. P-95 (66-81%) passes. Checked against P-269 Table 3 and P-95 Table 7.
reason: Both papers report three-class accuracy with 'normal/MCI/dementia' labels, but the labels are different constructs in different populations. P-269 bands community vaccine-centre attendees by their SLUMS screening score. P-95 uses clinical diagnoses of AD and MCI against matched healthy controls in a neurology clinic. So condition 1 fails. The numbers are far apart (93.3% against 66-81%), but P-269's figure is computed over the whole sample, most of which was training data, so it would need a held-out estimate before any comparison.

quotes.quote: This research conducted a cross-sectional study using in-person interviews with participants recruited from COVID vaccine centers in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia.

Based on the SLUMS Examination scores out of 30, the level of the patient’s cognitive problems was categorized as (i) Normal (score 25–30), (ii) MCI (Mild Cognitive Impairment) (score 20–24), (iii) dementia (score 0–19).

the first part consisted of three socio-demographic questions; the second part included four questions measuring the patient’s sleeping routine; the third part consisted of nine questions to explore the patient’s medical history.
The data were randomly allocated to training (80%) and testing (20%) datasets.
